title: CJP Launches 'School Thik Karo' Campaign to Fix Rural Government Schools
excerpt: The Cockroach Janta Party has announced a nationwide citizen-led campaign to audit and improve infrastructure in rural government schools, deploying community volunteers to assess electricity, water, sanitation, and mid-day meal quality.
body:
• CJP has launched "School Thik Karo," a nationwide campaign deploying volunteers to audit rural government schools for basic infrastructure
  • Volunteers will assess schools on four criteria: electricity, clean drinking water, functional washrooms, and mid-day meal standards
  • The "Sarpanch Challenge" encourages coordination with village-level elected representatives to carry out repairs within 30 days
  • CJP targets improvements in at least 100 schools within two months as a replicable model
  • Approximately 94,000 government schools have closed in India over the past decade, according to NITI Aayog data

From Protest to Ground-Level Action

The Cockroach Janta Party, the youth-led movement that forced Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan's resignation in July over exam paper leak allegations, has pivoted from street protests to direct community action. The group on Wednesday announced "School Thik Karo," a citizen-led campaign aimed at improving infrastructure in rural government schools across India.

https://x.com/IndiaToday/status/2087883343677497634

"Our focus is now entirely on constructive, ground-level action," CJP founder-president Abhijeet Dipke said in a statement, according to DY365. The 30-year-old Boston University graduate said the group intended to move beyond highlighting problems on social media toward working directly with communities.

How the Campaign Works

At the core of "School Thik Karo" is what CJP calls the "Sarpanch Challenge." The initiative encourages parents and young volunteers to inspect local schools and coordinate with sarpanches and panchayats — the elected heads and governing bodies of village-level local government — to carry out repairs.

Volunteers will assess schools against four criteria: availability of electricity, clean drinking water, functional washrooms, and the standard of mid-day meals. The group is also pushing for improved rural school transport, citing long walking distances faced by children during monsoon and peak summer months, according to DY365.

Audit findings, documented via mobile phones, will be submitted to local authorities. Community volunteers will then track whether repairs are completed within a stated 30-day window. CJP's initial target is to see improvements in at least 100 schools within two months, which it hopes to use as a model for wider replication.

The Broader Education Crisis

The campaign arrives against the backdrop of staggering school closure numbers. According to a widely reported NITI Aayog assessment and a written reply the Ministry of Education provided in the Lok Sabha, approximately 93,000 to 94,000 government schools closed between 2014-15 and 2024-25. Government data from UDISE+ reports has attributed the closures primarily to school rationalisation — the merging of institutions with low enrollment into nearby schools, according to DY365.

CJP has contrasted expenditure on projects such as the new Parliament building and the Prime Minister's residence with what it called systematic neglect of rural school infrastructure. The organisation said its campaign was not directed at any particular political party and appealed to MLAs and MPs to prioritise school infrastructure ahead of Independence Day.

"The fight for the soul of rural India's education has officially begun."

— Abhijeet Dipke, CJP Founder-President

From Exam Protests to Education Reform

CJP's rapid trajectory — from its founding in May 2026 as a satirical response to a remark by the Chief Justice of India, to amassing over 30 million followers and forcing a cabinet minister's resignation — has drawn both admiration and skepticism, according to Reuters and CNN. Critics, including some ruling BJP supporters, have questioned whether the movement's online reach can translate into sustained on-ground mobilisation.

The group's earlier protests at Jantar Mantar in New Delhi drew tens of thousands of demonstrators and the support of prominent activist Sonam Wangchuk, who undertook a 26-day hunger strike. After Pradhan's resignation in late July, CJP withdrew its agitation but signaled it would shift focus to constructive campaigns, according to The Hindu Business Line.

What Comes Next

Neither the Union Ministry of Education nor state panchayati raj departments had issued a formal response to the campaign at the time of CJP's announcement. Government officials have in the past pointed to existing central schemes — including Samagra Shiksha and PM SHRI — as ongoing efforts to upgrade rural school infrastructure.

CJP has not detailed how many volunteers have signed up or how audit findings will be verified before submission to authorities. The campaign's success will likely depend on whether its massive digital following can be channeled into the village-by-village school inspections the initiative demands. Dipke said the campaign would begin with volunteers, including himself, conducting audits in their own villages.
image_caption: CJP has launched a nationwide campaign to audit and improve rural government schools across India.
nri_angle: CJP's shift from exam protests to grassroots education reform signals a maturing youth movement with implications for India's broader governance and the diaspora's engagement with homeland issues.
